evidence: queue_consumer.py:144-149 does log and mark the offset complete after a failure, but that is deliberate and matches the existing behavior. The processor passed in is ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py:44-54), which already catches every Exception and logs 'Failed to process message result', so exceptions almost never reach the worker. The serial path (RunTask + CommitOffsets, result_consumer.py:214-217) and the batched path also commit after a logged failure. If failed offsets were never completed, get_committable_offsets (queue_consumer.py:89-93) would stop at that gap and the partition would never commit again. This is the same at-most-once-on-error behavior the consumer already has, not new data loss.

mark_committed (queue_consumer.py:100-105) only sets a dict entry and rebuilds a set comprehension of ints under a lock, so there is no realistic way for it to fail. Even if it did, the next _commit_loop pass would just commit the same or a higher offset again (queue_consumer.py:278-289). Kafka commits are idempotent, so the result would be one redundant commit, not an inconsistency that matters.

queue_consumer.py:49-54 uses dict.setdefault, which exists precisely to avoid this get-or-create race. On a builtin dict, setdefault is atomic in CPython: under the GIL, and with per-dict locking in free-threaded builds. If two threads race, the losing thread's new Lock is discarded and both threads get back the same stored lock. Separate locks cannot end up being used.

In submit (queue_consumer.py:293-325), self.queue_pool.submit(...) at line 315 is the last statement in the try block, so nothing after a successful submit can raise and reach the except. Inside FixedQueuePool.submit (queue_consumer.py:204-212), work_queue.put is the last call. If put raises (for example queue.ShutDown), the item was never enqueued, so completing its offset in the except block is correct. A successfully queued item cannot also be marked complete by the except path.

The worker calls work_queue.get() with no timeout and catches queue.ShutDown (queue_consumer.py:131-133). FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) (queue_consumer.py:236-240). Since Python 3.13, Queue.shutdown wakes threads blocked in get(), which raise ShutDown once the queue is empty. The repo pins Python 3.13.1 (.python-version). Workers therefore exit cleanly after draining, and they are daemon threads joined with a 5s timeout anyway (queue_consumer.py:242-243).

_commit_loop (queue_consumer.py:273-291) waits 1s before its first check. At startup nothing has been processed, so there is nothing to commit, and later commits are periodic anyway. A 1-second commit delay has no effect on correctness or throughput. Separately, though not what this comment claims, close() (queue_consumer.py:335-338) sets shutdown_event and the loop exits without a final commit pass. That is a different, unflagged concern.
